newsitem.title: CHINA: France's Chirac clinches China plane deals.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac clinches China plane deals.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac launched the first day of a state visit to China on Thursday with a rallying cry to make Beijing a major partner for the 21st century and the signing of some $1.8 billion in contracts.

Crowning Chirac's first day in China was a $1.5 billion deal by Airbus Industrie -- reached only after tortuous talks that stretched into the early hours of Thursday -- to sell 10 A320 and 20 A321 planes to Chinese airlines.
"China must be one of our main partners," Chirac, the first French president to visit China in 14 years, told French businessmen on the first day of his four-day visit.

"The China of tomorrow...will be one of the top nations of the world," he said. "I should like all my compatriots to share my conviction that despite the geographical distance between us, China must be one of our main partners."

President Jiang Zemin smiled broadly as he greeted Chirac at the Great Hall of the People, welcoming and praising the European head of state who has taken a lead in playing down criticism of China's human rights record and opposing a western move this year to censure Beijing in the United Nations.
During their 105-minute meeting, Jiang described as a "wise decision" French opposition to censuring China over human rights and a Paris decision to curb arms sales to Taiwan.
However, France's Foreign Minister Herve de Charette was expected to raise individual human rights cases on Friday.

Sino-French relations soured in the early 1990s over sales of French jet fighters and frigates to China's rival, Taiwan, but have recovered since Paris pledged in 1994 to end arms sales to the island that Beijing considers a rebel province.
Jiang and Chirac found plenty of common ground not just with a series of lucrative business deals but in their approach to the superpower position of the United States.
"Both sides...are opposed to any attempt to dominate (international affairs)," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Tang Guoqiang said in apparent reference to the United States.
Chirac echoed one of Jiang's favourite themes with a call for a multi-polar world, one without a single superpower.
"The bi-polar world no longer exists and a multi-polar world is taking shape," state television quoted Chirac as telling Jiang. "We should promote this and strengthen ties."
France and Europe needed new ideas and a new approach in dealing with China, Chirac said.

Establishing a "comprehensive partnership" would be the major theme of a joint communique to be signed by Chirac and Jiang on Friday and which will state the need for annual exchanges by heads of state and for stronger ties.
China's "comprehensive partnership" with France shared common features with Beijing's "strategic partnership" with Russia, the Chinese spokesman said.
However, business was the order of Chirac's first day.

Airbus Industrie signed a $1.5 billion deal to sell 30 planes to Chinese airlines as well as a contract with Aviation Industries of China, Alenia of Italy's Finmeccanica and Singapore Technologies Aerospace to manufacture a 100-seat jet. That project, to be in production by 2003, is expected to require investment of $2.0 billion.

Alenia, as part of an aircraft marketing consortium that also comprises Aerospatiale of France and British Aerospace Plc, signed an $80 million contract to sell five ATR-72 aircraft, with options on five more.

Rhone-Poulenc signed a 500 million franc ($88 million) joint venture to produce pesticide, Lafarge raised its stake in a cement joint venture by $75 million and China broke ground on the Ling'ao nuclear power plant near Hong Kong, for which Framatome is supplying the main nuclear reactors.
